findings.title: Global cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
findings.body: The ticker that drives CleanUpService.clean() is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This does not only affect annotation cleanup: the same clean() run executes temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, user-invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup. All of those jobs will now run ten times as often, increasing database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance, and the PR description gives no reason for this unrelated change. It looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or justified separately.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
findings.body: The new batch loops in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) call r.log.Error unconditionally, including on success where the logged err value is nil. Every batch of a routine cleanup will therefore emit error-level log lines, which pollutes logs, can trigger error alerting, and prints the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes) on every iteration. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug and should not dump the full ID list.

findings.title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, so large batches still fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL
findings.body: deleteByIDs special-cases only SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999; for all other databases it builds one DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with len(ids) bound parameters. PostgreSQL's extended protocol allows at most 65535 parameters per statement (MySQL has similar placeholder/packet limits), so a configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup batch fail, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter-count limit regardless of batch size. The workaround should be based on the actual number of IDs and the target dialect's limit, chunk the DELETE, or inline IDs for large batches on all dialects.

findings.title: Split SELECT/DELETE for MaxCount can delete annotations that are back within the retention count
findings.body: For MaxCount cleanup, IDs are selected with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount and then deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If one of the newest MaxCount annotations is deleted (e.g. via the annotation Delete API) between the SELECT and the DELETE, a fetched ID moves into the set that should now be retained, but it is still deleted, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations. The old single-statement DELETE evaluated the offset atomically. The PR description only acknowledges under-deletion on concurrent inserts; this concurrent-delete path causes over-deletion beyond the configured retention policy.

findings.title: SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf string concatenation
findings.body: In the SQLite large-batch branch, values is grown with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. This copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration, making building the IN list O(n^2); with the newly tested batch size of 32767 IDs the final string is hundreds of kilobytes and is re-copied tens of thousands of times. Use strings.Builder (or strconv.AppendInt into a []byte) to build the list in linear time.
